linkedin:
Every QRON code's visual pattern comes from a deterministic seed: hash the product's own identity — product ID, NFT token, serial number — and that hash drives the image-generation pipeline. Feed in the same identity twice, get the same pattern back. Change any one input — a different serial, a different token — and the pattern changes too.

The consequence: a counterfeiter who lifts a QR payload and re-prints it on a different unit can't just swap the destination and call it done. The pattern on the copy no longer matches what that unit's actual identity would generate, so a mismatch between pattern and identity is something that can, in principle, be checked — not just whatever the URL resolves to. Each code is also Ed25519-signed and anchored under the AuthiChain protocol, so the signature — not the seed's secrecy — is what carries the real security property; the pattern layers a second, visual signal on top.

We built it this way because a QR code by itself is just a container: whatever's encoded in it gets trusted at face value the moment someone scans it. Deriving the visual pattern from the product's own identity, deterministically, ties the artwork itself to the same identity the signature protects.

If you're issuing per-unit codes today and the only check happening at scan time is "does the URL load," take a look at what a signed, identity-derived code adds.

reddit.title: QRON's QR artwork is deterministic — the pattern is a hash of the product's identity, not random art
reddit.body:
QRON's QR-code artwork runs through an image-generation pipeline, but the seed isn't random: it's a hash of the product's own identity (product ID, NFT token, serial number). Same identity in, same pattern out, on every run, deterministically — no randomness anywhere in the seed derivation.

That means the pattern is reproducible and checkable: given the identity data, anyone running the same pipeline gets the same artwork back. Separately, each code is Ed25519-signed and the signature is anchored under the AuthiChain protocol — the signature is what actually carries the security property, not secrecy of the seed derivation. A lifted QR payload re-printed on a different unit produces a pattern that doesn't match that unit's real identity, so the mismatch is a second thing to check beyond the signature itself.

Pushback welcome: is there a cleaner way to think about pairing a deterministic visual seed with a signature scheme, or is the pattern mostly cosmetic once the signature is doing the real verification work? Also curious whether tying the seed to identity data creates any correlation or privacy tradeoff worth flagging.

https://qron.space/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=qron-visual-fingerprint&utm_content=b

Disclosure: I work on this project.
